meta.description: Earliest known: Texas Tech's Ralph Carpenter in the Dallas Morning News, March 10, 1976. Built on older church sayings; Dan Cook was also credited.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It Ain’t Over ’Til the Fat Lady Sings'?
meta.ogDescription: Earliest record: Ralph Carpenter, Dallas Morning News, 1976: “The opera ain’t over until the fat lady sings.” Quote Investigator credits him provisionally.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: Texas Tech University sports information director (1976)
answer.sourceLine: The earliest known “opera/fat lady” version is Carpenter’s remark in the Dallas Morning News of March 10, 1976: “The opera ain’t over until the fat lady sings.” Quote Investigator credits him only provisionally. The saying grew out of much older “church ain’t out till the singing’s done” proverbs, a 1978 report credited sportscaster Dan Cook instead, and the shorter “It ain’t over” wording is not the form Carpenter is recorded as using.

Ralph Carpenter, Texas Tech sports information director

source.excerpt: Despite his obvious allegiance to the Red Raiders, Texas Tech sports information director Ralph Carpenter was the picture of professional objectivity when the Aggies rallied for a 72-72 tie late in the SWC tournament finals. … “Right,” said Ralph, “The opera ain’t over until the fat lady sings.”
trail: Quote Investigator (2015) ↗ traces the family of sayings back to an 1872 newspaper (“As long as the organ is playing church is not out”). It concludes that in the earliest published evidence, dated March 10, 1976, Ralph Carpenter spoke the phrase, and it “would provisionally credit” him.

Fred Shapiro, editor of the Yale Book of Quotations, first reported the Dallas Morning News citation in a 2005 ADS-L post ↗. He said it “calls into question the usual attribution of the phrase to Dan Cook.”
Shapiro also found “Church ain’t out ’till the fat lady sings” in a 1976 booklet, Southern Words and Sayings, which points to Southern folk sayings as a possible source (ADS-L ↗; QI ↗).

A June 3, 1978 Washington Post article credited San Antonio sports editor Dan Cook with the line circa 1975. QI ↗ calls that claim “difficult to evaluate because no details were provided about the evidence.”
source.excerptNote: From Fred Shapiro’s transcription of the newspaper item, posted to the American Dialect Society mailing list on September 6, 2005. One garbled line of the transcription is left out (…). Note that Carpenter’s recorded words begin “The opera ain’t over,” not “It ain’t over.”

author.name: Ralph Carpenter
author.heading: About Ralph Carpenter
author.metaLine: Fl. 1976 · Texas Tech University sports information director
author.bio: Ralph Carpenter was the sports information director at Texas Tech University when the Dallas Morning News quoted him during a close Southwest Conference tournament basketball final against Texas A&M in March 1976. Yale librarian Fred Shapiro found that newspaper item, and Quote Investigator ↗ now provisionally credits Carpenter with the modern “opera ain’t over until the fat lady sings” adage.

misattribution.heading: Who else gets the credit
misattribution.intro: Several sports figures have been named as the source of this saying, and Yogi Berra popularized a similar but separate line. Today’s popular wording, “It ain’t over ’til the fat lady sings,” is not the form found in the 1976 record, which begins “The opera ain’t over.”

items.why: A 1978 Washington Post article credited the San Antonio sports editor and sportscaster, and a 1980 New York Times answer said he had used it “for a number of years.” The Post placed his use circa 1975, but Quote Investigator ↗ found no evidence given for that date.
The Washington Bullets coach made the line famous during the 1978 NBA playoffs. In a May 9, 1978 UPI report he himself said he had heard it from “a Texas sportscaster” (QI ↗).

Berra popularized “It ain’t over till it’s over,” which Wikipedia ↗ lists among phrases with a similar meaning, as a variation of the baseball saying “The game isn’t over until the final out.” It is a separate saying.

Sayings that church isn’t out until the singing stops appear in print from 1872. The “fat lady” turns up in a church version, “Church ain’t out ’till the fat lady sings,” in the 1976 booklet Southern Words and Sayings (QI ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest published “opera/fat lady” version is Ralph Carpenter’s, in the Dallas Morning News of March 10, 1976. Quote Investigator ↗ credits him provisionally and notes the saying grew out of a much older family of church-and-singing proverbs.

context.heading: Why the fat lady?
lead: Long before opera came into it, Americans said a contest wasn’t settled until the singing was done. The comparison was to a church service, which isn’t over until the last hymn. Quote Investigator ↗ found it applied to a presidential race in 1872, and it was common in politics and sports for decades afterward.

The opera version swaps the closing hymn for a soprano’s finale. Wikipedia ↗ notes it is generally understood as a nod to heavyset opera sopranos, and often to Wagner’s Brünnhilde, whose farewell scene leads into the finale of the Ring cycle.
